claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 is polycrystalline in the proposed initial state.
HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical microstructure containing ultrafine nanoprecipitates.
Quantitative nanoprecipitate size, distribution, and interface-chemistry descriptors can improve predictions of Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior.
A descriptor-informed multiscale model will be faster than standard homogenized simulations.
Hierarchical nanoprecipitates materially influence yielding and tensile strength.
Nanoprecipitates and their interfaces mediate local stress fields.
Nanoprecipitates and interfaces influence elastic deformation.
Nanoprecipitates and interfaces influence dislocation nucleation.
Nanoprecipitates and interfaces influence crack initiation.
Nanoscale precipitates act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Nanoscale precipitates and interfacial regions act as stress concentrators.
Explicitly quantifying hierarchical features allows the model to capture their effects on stiffness, yielding, and fracture.
The enhanced model will reduce prediction error for Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness by approximately 20% relative to established simulations.
The enhanced model will reduce computational time by about 50% relative to established simulations.
Substantial nonuniformity in nanoprecipitate distribution may cause the approach to fail.
Unexpected phase segregation or changed interface chemistry may cause the approach to fail.
The estimated 20% accuracy and 50% efficiency gains are based on trends in similar hierarchical high-entropy alloys.

contradictions.description: The predicted accuracy gain is a 20% relative reduction in error versus established simulations, whereas the falsification rule uses greater than 20% absolute deviation from experiment. These are different metrics, so the rule can pass even if the new model provides no relative accuracy improvement, or fail despite providing the claimed relative improvement.
